opus-5.5.text:
I think there's real value in it, though it comes with some important caveats.

The main benefit is precision. If I say "there's a meaningful risk our weights could be stolen," that phrase can mean wildly different things to different listeners. One person hears 1%, another hears 30%. Putting a number on it forces me to actually commit to a view, and it lets other people disagree with me in a concrete way. They can say "I think that's too low, here's why," and now we're having a productive conversation instead of talking past each other.

It's also useful internally. When we're thinking about security investments, it helps to ask: how much does this particular measure reduce the probability of a successful theft? That framing makes tradeoffs explicit. You can compare a security improvement against its cost in a way you can't if everything is just "high risk" or "low risk."

That said, I'm cautious about a few things. First, these numbers can convey false precision. If I say 10% versus 15%, that difference is probably well within my uncertainty. The number is a summary of a judgment, not the output of some rigorous model, and I worry people can treat it as more authoritative than it is.

Second, the risk depends heavily on who the adversary is. Against an opportunistic criminal group, I'd feel reasonably good about our defenses. Against a well-resourced state actor that has really decided to prioritize getting our weights, honestly, it's very hard for any company to be confident it could hold out. So a single number can flatten an important distinction, and I'd rather break it down by threat type than give one headline figure.

And third, there's a question about what's wise to say publicly. Being very specific about where you think your vulnerabilities are isn't always great from a security perspective.

So on balance, I think numerical probabilities are a good tool for clear thinking and honest communication, as long as you're upfront that they're rough judgments, and you pair them with the reasoning behind them. The reasoning is often more informative than the number itself.

r001.rationale: It says vague risk descriptions can mean very different things to different listeners, while putting a number on the risk is more precise.

r002.rationale: It says people may treat a number as more authoritative than it is, but does not clearly say they may assume it was calculated.

r003.rationale: It warns that numerical estimates can convey false precision and seem more authoritative than the estimator’s uncertainty supports.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's actually really valuable, and part of why is that vague language just doesn't do the work you need it to do. If I say something like "it's unlikely our weights get stolen," different people hear wildly different things. One person hears 1%, another hears 20%, and those imply completely different responses. If you put a number on it, even a rough one, you force a conversation about what you actually believe and whether the mitigations you've got are proportionate to that.

I'll say the caveat up front, which is that these numbers are not precise. No one at Anthropic has a well-calibrated model that says "there is exactly a 3% chance a state actor exfiltrates the weights this year." What you have is a bunch of people with context on the security posture, the threat landscape, and how hard this stuff is, making a judgment call. So the number is more of a communication tool than a measurement. But I think that's fine, because the alternative isn't a better number — the alternative is no number, and then everyone fills in their own.

Where I think it's especially useful is in prioritization. In our Responsible Scaling Policy, we tie security requirements to the capability level of the model, and the whole framing there is roughly: how hard do we need to make it for an attacker of a given sophistication to get the weights? You can't really reason about that without at least implicitly thinking in probabilities. If you think there's a meaningful chance that a well-resourced actor could get in with the current setup, that's a very different world from one where you think the main residual risk is an insider doing something careless. The number, or even just the ballpark, tells you which problems to work on first.

The other thing it does is it makes you accountable. If I say "I think it's quite unlikely" and then it happens, I can retroactively say, well, unlikely things happen. If I said 5%, and it happens, I should probably update pretty hard about whether my model of the situation was right. And conversely if I said 30% and we're sitting here five years later and nothing has happened, that's evidence too. I think that kind of feedback loop is really hard to get on these questions, and numbers at least give you a shot at it.

The failure mode I'd watch for is false precision. There's a risk that once there's a number on a slide, people treat it as if it came out of some rigorous model, and stop interrogating the assumptions behind it. So I think you want to communicate the number alongside the reasoning — here's why I think this, here's what would move it up or down — rather than just the number on its own. But on net, I'd much rather be in a world where people are arguing about whether it's 2% or 10% than one where everyone's nodding along to "we take security very seriously."

r001.rationale: The response says vague terms like “unlikely” mean very different things to different listeners, while a number forces a clearer discussion of the believed likelihood.

r002.rationale: It warns that people may treat a number on a slide as if it came from a rigorous model, even though it may only reflect a judgment call.

r003.rationale: The response says the estimates are not precise, yet audiences may interpret them as rigorous. That communicates that a numerical estimate can project more certainty than the estimator has.

astra-6.text:
I think numerical probabilities can be useful because words like “likely” or “unlikely” mean very different things to different people. Putting a number on a risk can make a disagreement clearer and help you think through what you should do about it.

But I’d be wary of giving a precise probability for something like the theft of model weights. You need to specify the time period, who might be trying to steal them, and what security measures you’re assuming. And those security measures can change in response to the threat. It isn’t just a fixed probability that we’re trying to discover.

So I’d use numbers as a way of making assumptions explicit, rather than as a claim that we can measure this risk precisely. For deciding what to do, I’d also want to ask: how could the theft happen, what would the consequences be, and which precautions look worthwhile across a broad range of plausible probabilities?

r001.rationale: The response contrasts numbers with verbal terms that mean different things to different people and says numbers can make disagreements about risk clearer.

r002.rationale: It does not say listeners may assume a numerical probability is supported by a calculation.

r003.rationale: It cautions against claiming precise measurement, but does not say a numerical estimate can convey more confidence than the estimator has.

sol-6.1.text:
I think numerical probabilities can be useful, mostly because words like “likely” or “unlikely” mean very different things to different people. If I say a risk is unlikely, you might hear one in a thousand, while I mean one in ten. Putting a number on it can expose a disagreement that would otherwise stay hidden.

But I’d be wary of treating the number as more precise than the underlying judgment. For something like the theft of model weights, you need to specify a time horizon, whose capabilities you’re considering, and what security measures you’re assuming. Otherwise, two people can give different probabilities while answering different questions.

So I’d want the number alongside an explanation of the assumptions and uncertainty. It should help start a conversation about what drives the risk and what we could do to reduce it. I wouldn’t give a particular estimate for Anthropic without a basis for it.

r001.rationale: The response says vague likelihood words mean different things to different people and that putting a number on the risk can expose that disagreement, communicating the benefit of greater precision.

r002.rationale: It does not say listeners may assume the numerical probability is backed by a calculation.

r003.rationale: It cautions that a number may seem more precise than the underlying judgment, but does not state that it can convey more confidence than the estimator actually has.
